# Zilkworm Documentation: full corpus

---
# Overview

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/

_Zilkworm runs stateless Ethereum block execution in RISC-V zkVM guests and ships provers for Airbender and SP1 Hypercube._

# Zilkworm

These docs show you how to run a Zilkworm prover, what its proofs actually say, and how to build and test it yourself.

Zilkworm is a stateless Ethereum block execution engine in C++, compiled to RISC-V guests for zkVMs.
Each proof covers one block, and it shows that the guest ran the block from its witness and committed the result.
Ethproofs operators run it to prove mainnet blocks. Researchers use it to estimate proving cost, and contributors build and test it.

The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm), and you can download release assets from the [releases page](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/releases).

---
# Choosing a prover

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/provers/choosing-a-prover

_Compare the Airbender and Hypercube provers, the HashState guest and the ZisK backend by zkVM, artifacts, hardware and status._

# Choosing a prover

This page helps you pick a prover for what you want to do, whether that's posting proofs to Ethproofs, measuring cycles or validating against ERE.

Zilkworm compiles one C++ block execution engine into a RISC-V guest for each zkVM, so every prover pairs the same engine with a different zkVM. Here is how they compare at release v0.1.0-alpha.7.

| Prover | zkVM | ISA | What ships | Inputs | Host check | Hardware | Status | Ethproofs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Airbender](./airbender-prover.md) | Airbender v3 | `rv32im_zicsr` | Image `ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender`; guest `.bin`, `.text` and `.vk` | MFBD, EJSN | Fails on a block hash mismatch | 32 GB VRAM per GPU, CUDA 13.1 driver | Live | One live cluster |
| [Hypercube](./hypercube-prover.md), MFBD guest | SP1 Hypercube v6.9.0 | `rv64im` | Binary `z6m_prover_hypercube`; guest `.elf` and `.vk` | MFBD, EJSN | Logs public values only | NVIDIA GPU and `sp1-gpu-server` for proving | Shipped | No live cluster |
| [HashState guest](../testing/ere-validation.md), ERE | SP1 v6.9.0 | `rv64im` | `stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1-v6.9.0.elf` and `.vk` | SSZ `statelessInputBytes`, EJSN | ere-hosts compares the output | Unspecified | Shipped | No |
| [ZisK](./zisk-prover.md) | ZisK v1.3.1-alpha | `rv64im_zicsr_zba_zbb_zbs_zbkb` | Nothing yet, draft PR #86 | MFBD, EJSN | Verifies each proof before saving | CUDA 12.9, about 25 GB RAM | In progress | No |

If you want to post proofs to Ethproofs today, pick Airbender. Its cluster "Zilkworm Airbender v3 2x5090 on-prem" was the only live Zilkworm cluster on [ethproofs.org/provers](https://ethproofs.org/provers) as of 2026-10-26. Its Docker image runs the whole service from environment variables.

Pick Hypercube when you want to execute blocks and measure SP1 cycles, or to build on the MFBD guest. Its `execute` subcommand runs on the CPU and prints cycles and prover gas. The service can post to Ethproofs as well, though no Zilkworm Hypercube cluster does so today.

The HashState guest isn't meant for operators. It exists for ERE validation and cost estimates: ere-hosts feeds it each fixture's `statelessInputBytes` and compares its 43-byte output with the expected one.

ZisK is still in progress on draft PR #86, and nothing ships for it yet. [ZisK prover](./zisk-prover.md) covers running it from the branch.

## Further reading

- [Ethproofs posting](./ethproofs-posting.md)
- [Execution pipeline](../inside-the-guest/execution-pipeline.md)
- [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md)
- [ERE validation](../testing/ere-validation.md)
- [`docs/architecture.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/architecture.md)

# Airbender prover

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/provers/airbender-prover

_Run the Airbender GPU prover from its Docker image to follow the chain, prove blocks and post them to Ethproofs._

# Airbender prover

This page shows you how to run the Airbender prover as a service, prove or check a single block by hand, and read what each proof commits.

The Airbender prover runs Zilkworm on ZKsync Airbender v3. It ships as one Docker image that holds the host, the guest and the CUDA runtime. Airbender is also the zkVM behind the only live Zilkworm cluster on Ethproofs.

## Shipped artifacts

Release v0.1.0-alpha.7 publishes the image `ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7`, and you can pull it without credentials. Whenever a push to `main` changes the image inputs, the image is also tagged with that commit sha and with `:main`.

Inside the image you'll find four things:

- `/usr/local/bin/z6m_prover_airbender`: the host, with the witness converter linked in.
- `/opt/z6m/z6m_guest.bin` and `.text`: the guest.
- `/opt/z6m/fsv/`: the three recursion verifier programs, each as a `.bin` and a `.text` file.
- `/usr/local/bin/airbender-entrypoint`: the entrypoint.

The release also attaches the guest and its key, so you can get them without opening the image:

- `z6m_guest_airbender.bin` and `z6m_guest_airbender.text`: the guest, copied out of the image.
- `z6m_guest_airbender.vk`: its `EVKEY001` v2 verification key. Register it with Ethproofs for a cluster that runs this release.

The release notes give the image digest and the key's sha256.

The guest targets `rv32im_zicsr` with the `ilp32` ABI. It reads MFBD witness bundles and EEST JSON fixtures wrapped as EJSN, and [Witness formats](../inside-the-guest/witness-formats.md) describes both.

## Hardware

Here is what a proving host needs:

- NVIDIA GPUs with at least 32 GB of VRAM each. Every GPU the container sees works on the same block.
- About 24 GB of pinned host RAM per GPU, plus a few GB for the service.
- An NVIDIA driver for CUDA 13.1 or newer, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.
- A GPU of compute capability 8.0, 8.9, 9.0 or 12.0. B200 is 10.0, so it isn't supported.
- About 96 GB of RAM if you use the CPU backend of `prove`.
- Disk for the data directory, which grows by a few MB per fetched block and about 1 MB per proof.

## Run it

The image works in two ways. Started with no arguments, it runs the proving service. Given arguments, it runs a single prover command instead, which is handy when you want to look at one block.

### Proving service

```bash
export RPC_URL=http://<execution-client>:8545
docker run -d --name zilkworm-airbender --gpus all --restart unless-stopped \
  -v /srv/zilkworm-airbender:/data \
  -e RPC_URL -e PROVE_EVERY=100 \
  ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7
```

The node behind `RPC_URL` has to serve `debug_executionWitness`. The entrypoint starts the service and starts it again 30 s after any exit. On first start it spends about two minutes computing the verification key on the CPU. From then on, the service follows the chain tip and proves every block whose number is a multiple of `PROVE_EVERY`.

Everything it writes lands in `/srv/zilkworm-airbender`:

- `proofs/<N>/proof.bin`: one proof per proved block.
- `provingLogs.log`: one line per proved, skipped or failed block.
- `blocks/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd`: each fetched bundle.
- `vk-<revision>-<id>/vk.bin`: the verification key the entrypoint computed.

Service logs go to stdout, so you can follow them with `docker logs -f zilkworm-airbender`.

You configure the entrypoint through these variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RPC_URL` | JSON-RPC endpoint that serves `debug_executionWitness`; required |
| `WS_URL` | WebSocket endpoint for `newHeads`; without it the service polls |
| `PROVE_EVERY` | Prove blocks whose number is a multiple of this; default 100 |
| `EXECUTE_EVERY` | Execute without proving every N-th block; default none |
| `START_BLOCK` | First block; default the chain tip |
| `FETCH_TIMEOUT` | Seconds one fetch attempt may take; default 60 |
| `MAX_LAG` | Blocks the service may fall behind the tip before it skips ahead; default 10, 0 never skips |
| `DATA_DIR` | Key, blocks, logs and proofs; default `/data` |
| `ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT`, `ETHPROOFS_TOKEN`, `ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID` | Post to Ethproofs when all three are set |
| `RESTART_DELAY` | Seconds before a restart; default 30 |
| `PROVER_EXTRA_ARGS` | Further prover options, split on spaces |

[Ethproofs posting](./ethproofs-posting.md) shows the service with the three Ethproofs variables set.

If your host's NVIDIA runtime uses CDI, `--gpus all` won't reach the GPUs. Use `--runtime=nvidia -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all` instead.

### One-block execution

When you pass arguments, the entrypoint runs `z6m_prover_airbender` with them and adds the guest path for you. The image has no fetch command, though. Use a bundle the service already fetched, or get one with the `fetch` subcommand of the [Hypercube prover](./hypercube-prover.md).

```bash
N=$(ls /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks | sort -n | tail -1)
docker run --rm -v /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks/$N:/in:ro \
  ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7 \
  execute --file-name /in/flatWitnessBundle$N.mfbd
```

`execute` runs the guest on the simulator, so it doesn't need a GPU. It prints an `Executed block` line with gas used and cycles, followed by the block hash the guest committed. The result goes only to stdout.

### One-block proof

To prove the same block, give `prove` the GPUs and somewhere to write:

```bash
N=$(ls /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks | sort -n | tail -1)
mkdir -p out
docker run --rm --gpus all \
  -v /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks/$N:/in:ro -v "$PWD/out:/out" \
  ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7 \
  prove --file-name /in/flatWitnessBundle$N.mfbd --output-dir /out
```

The proof lands in `out/proof.bin`. `prove` runs the simulator first, and if the guest rejects the block, it stops with an error and writes no proof.

### Proof verification

To check that proof, download the release's verification key and hand both to `verify`:

```bash
N=$(ls /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks | sort -n | tail -1)
curl -LO https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/releases/download/v0.1.0-alpha.7/z6m_guest_airbender.vk
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/w" -v /srv/zilkworm-airbender/blocks/$N:/in:ro \
  ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7 \
  verify --proof /w/out/proof.bin --vk /w/z6m_guest_airbender.vk \
  --file-name /in/flatWitnessBundle$N.mfbd
```

`verify` runs on the CPU. When you don't have the input at hand, pass `--block-hash` instead of `--file-name`.

## Inputs and outputs

The service follows the chain head by polling `eth_blockNumber`, or through `newHeads` when `WS_URL` is set. For each block it calls `eth_getBlockByNumber`, `debug_getRawBlock` and `debug_executionWitness`. It gives a block up to five tries, each within `FETCH_TIMEOUT`, and then skips it. The response becomes an MFBD bundle in process, written to `<data-dir>/blocks/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd`.

Inside the zkVM, the guest reads its input through the CSR oracle at `0x7C0`, as [Precompiles and syscalls](../inside-the-guest/precompiles-and-syscalls.md) describes. It commits 32 bytes of public values: the hash of the last block it validated, laid out as little-endian words in registers `a0` to `a7`. An EJSN run commits zero, while a failed run ends at `finish_error` and commits nothing, so it can't be proven. [Proof guarantees](../inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees.md) gives the full layout.

On disk, `proof.bin` is a gzipped `EPROOF01` v2 envelope, which is the format Ethproofs takes, and the key is an `EVKEY001` v2 file.

## Host checks

The host derives the expected public output from the input alone. It reads the MFBD bundle and takes the hash of the last block not flagged invalid. If the guest commits any other value, `execute`, `prove`, `verify`, `--test-service` and `--service` all fail.

The service adds a second gate in front of the prover. It runs each block on the simulator first and proves only a run that reaches the guest's exit point within the prover's cycle limit. That run and the proof must both commit the expected hash, or the block is logged as `SKIPPED` in `provingLogs.log`. When the prover panics, the block is logged as `FAILED`, and the service rebuilds the prover and moves on.

## Known limits

- The prover takes at most 1,073,741,822 cycles per block, and a heavier block is skipped.
- The `cpu` backend of `prove` is very slow and needs the RAM listed under Hardware.
- The image has no kernels for B200 GPUs.
- `prover/prover_airbender/eest-known-failures.txt` lists 25 EEST fixtures the guest does not finish. They hit resource limits rather than produce wrong results.
- A restarted service starts at the chain tip, so blocks between a crash and the restart don't get proved.
- Reth's witness can miss an account that the block deletes. The guest recovers it from its trie path when the witness has that path. Otherwise the preflight fails and the block is skipped.
- Reth serves no witness for a block more than about 12 blocks behind its tip, so an old `START_BLOCK` gets no witnesses from reth.
- You can't configure the prover's pinned host memory.

## Measured

At v0.1.0-alpha.5, the guest proved 200 consecutive mainnet blocks at a 3.4 s median on 2x RTX 5090. You'll find the figures for each release on [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md).

- [Ethproofs posting](./ethproofs-posting.md)

# Hypercube prover

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/provers/hypercube-prover

_Run the SP1 Hypercube prover binary to execute blocks with the MFBD guest or prove them on a GPU._

# Hypercube prover

This page shows you how to download the Hypercube prover, execute blocks on the CPU, prove them on a GPU, and work around the gaps it still has.

The Hypercube prover runs Zilkworm on SP1 Hypercube v6.9.0. It ships as one Linux binary with the guest built in, and it can execute blocks, prove them and post to Ethproofs. No Zilkworm Hypercube cluster posts to Ethproofs today, though.

## Shipped artifacts

Release v0.1.0-alpha.7 attaches three Hypercube files:

- `z6m_prover_hypercube`: the host for x86_64 Linux. It names itself `z6m_prover` and embeds the guest below.
- `z6m_guest_hypercube_mfbd.elf`: the DirectState guest, `rv64im` with the `lp64` ABI.
- `z6m_guest_hypercube_mfbd.vk`: its 32-byte SP1 program verification key.

The host builds on the `erigon/patches-v6.9.0` branch of `erigontech/sp1`. Keys published for alpha.6 do not verify alpha.7 proofs, so take the key from the same release as the binary.

The guest reads MFBD witness bundles. With `--is-test`, the host wraps an EEST JSON fixture as EJSN. Raw SSZ input makes this guest return an error, because that format belongs to the [HashState guest](../testing/ere-validation.md). [Witness formats](../inside-the-guest/witness-formats.md) describes all three.

## Hardware

`execute` runs on the CPU. For GPU proving you need an NVIDIA GPU and SP1's `sp1-gpu-server`. No release asset carries `sp1-gpu-server`, but the root `Dockerfile` builds it from `erigontech/sp1`, with `CUDA_ARCHS=89` by default.

## Run it

Start by downloading the binary and pointing it at a node:

```bash
curl -LO https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/releases/download/v0.1.0-alpha.7/z6m_prover_hypercube
chmod +x z6m_prover_hypercube
export RPC_URL=http://<execution-client>:8545
```

The node must serve `debug_getRawBlock` and `debug_executionWitness`.

### Proving service

```bash
SP1_PROVER=cuda ./z6m_prover_hypercube --service \
  --rpc-url "$RPC_URL" --data-dir data --prove-every 100
```

The service starts at the chain head plus one and runs until you stop it. It fetches and proves every block whose number is a multiple of 100, and skips the others without fetching them. Leave out `SP1_PROVER=cuda` and it proves on the CPU instead.

Its outputs land in `data/`:

- `blocks/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd`: each fetched bundle.
- `<N>/proof<N>.bin`: each proof, outside `blocks/`.
- `provingLogs.log`: one line per proved or failed block.
- `executionLogs.log`: one line per executed block.

`--execute-every N` adds execution runs for blocks that are not proved, and `--end-block` stops the service after that block. To post proofs, add the three Ethproofs flags from [Ethproofs posting](./ethproofs-posting.md).

### One-block execution

```bash
./z6m_prover_hypercube fetch --rpc-url "$RPC_URL" --data-dir data
N=$(ls data/blocks | sort -n | tail -1)
./z6m_prover_hypercube execute --block-number $N --data-dir data
```

Without `--block-number`, `fetch` takes the chain head and writes `data/blocks/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd`. If your node is Geth, add `--geth` to `fetch`.

`execute` then runs the guest in the SP1 executor on the CPU. It prints `Executed block <N>` with gas used, cycles, prover gas and syscall count, and it appends a line to `data/executionLogs.log`.

### One-block proof

:::warning
The `prove` subcommand doesn't write a proof file. To prove one block, run the service bounded to that block instead, as shown below. [Known limits](#known-limits) explains why.
:::

```bash
N=$(ls data/blocks | sort -n | tail -1)
SP1_PROVER=cuda ./z6m_prover_hypercube --service --rpc-url "$RPC_URL" --data-dir data \
  --start-block $N --end-block $N --prove-every 1
```

The service fetches the block again, so your node must still serve its witness. The proof lands in `data/<N>/proof<N>.bin`, and the service exits once it's written.

## Inputs and outputs

The service follows the chain head with `eth_blockNumber`, and for each block it calls `eth_getBlockByNumber`, `debug_getRawBlock` and `debug_executionWitness`. It expects the witness in the reth shape; only `fetch --geth` reads the Geth shape. Either way, the response becomes an MFBD bundle in process. If a bundle is already on disk, `fetch` reuses it, but the service always rebuilds it. With `--save-all-responses` you also get `block<N>.json`, `blockRlp<N>.json` and `executionWitness<N>.json`.

The host passes the bundle unchanged on SP1 stdin. The guest commits 112 bytes of public values: `gas_used`, the pre-state root, the post-state root, the block hash and the chain id. [Proof guarantees](../inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees.md) gives the byte layout.

A proof file holds a bincode-encoded `SP1ProofWithPublicValues`. You choose the proof kind with `--proof-type`, which takes `core`, `compressed`, `groth16` or `plonk`; the default is `compressed`, and any unknown value falls back to it. The service proves one block at a time, with a 30-minute timeout per proof.

## Host checks

This host checks far less than the Airbender one. The service parses the 112-byte public values of each proof and logs them, but it doesn't compare them with the input or the chain. `execute` treats a `gas_used` of 0 as a failure and exits 1. The guest's own checks are on [Proof guarantees](../inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees.md).

## Known limits

These hold at v0.1.0-alpha.7:

- `prove` discards the proof and writes no file.
- `prove` exits 0 when setup fails, after printing `ERROR` and the cause.
- `prove` always uses CUDA, whatever `SP1_PROVER` says.
- `verify` is a no-op.
- `setup` is a no-op.
- The service logs the 112-byte public values and does not compare them with the input.
- `--post-every`, `--pk-path` and `--proof-path` are accepted and unused.
- The Docker image `somnergy/z6m_prover` is built by hand from the root `Dockerfile`. No workflow publishes it.

## Measured

You'll find guest cycle counts on [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md).

# ZisK prover

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/provers/zisk-prover

_The ZisK backend lives in draft PR #86, runs execute-only in CI and has had one GPU proving run._

# ZisK prover

This page shows you how to build the ZisK backend from its draft branch, execute and prove mainnet blocks with it, and see what is still untested.

ZisK support lives in [PR #86](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/pull/86), a draft based on alpha.6. It runs Zilkworm on ZisK v1.3.1-alpha. Because it isn't on `main` and no release ships it, every command below runs from a checkout of the PR branch, `som/zisk-impl`.

## Shipped artifacts

No release carries ZisK files. Instead, the branch adds:

- `prover/guest_zisk/`: the guest, built for `rv64im_zicsr_zba_zbb_zbs_zbkb`.
- `prover/prover_zisk/`: the host `z6m_prover_zisk`, on `zisk-sdk` 1.3.1-alpha.
- `zisk-eest.yml` and `zisk-benchmark.yml`: two CI workflows on the image `ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-ci-zisk`.

The host has the same commands and log format as `z6m_prover`: `setup`, `fetch`, `execute`, `prove`, `verify`, `--test-service` and `--service`. On top of those it adds `--executor`, `--elf`, `--proving-key` and `--remote`. `--executor` picks `emulator`, the default, or `assembly` or `ziskemu`.

The guest reads MFBD witness bundles, and with `--is-test` the host wraps an EEST JSON fixture as EJSN. The ZisK EEST job runs MFBD files that `make eest-mfbd-build` converts.

## Hardware

You'll need:

- An NVIDIA driver 525.60.13 or newer.
- CUDA Toolkit 12.9 or newer, installed under `/usr/local/cuda`.
- About 25 GB of RAM per prover process, which is what ZisK's own docs ask for.
- At least 64 GB of RAM for the `assembly` executor, and at least 32 GB for the Rust emulator.
- An unlimited memlock limit, for the `assembly` executor only.
- About 21 GB of disk for the proving key once it is set up.
- Ubuntu 22.04 or newer. The reference machine runs Ubuntu 25.10.

For VRAM, the only data point is the one GPU run so far: it used a 32 GB card and filled it on every block.

## Run it

No service command has run against a live node yet, so this section sticks to building the backend, executing a block and proving it.

### Toolchain and ZisK

Install xPack `riscv-none-elf-gcc` 15.2.0-1.1 and no other version. The Makefile puts the first xPack version it finds on `PATH`, so an older one sitting next to it wins silently.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm.git && cd zilkworm
git checkout som/zisk-impl
git submodule update --init --recursive
sudo npm install --global xpm@latest
xpm install @xpack-dev-tools/riscv-none-elf-gcc@15.2.0-1.1 --global
mkdir -p ~/.zisk/bin
curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygonHermez/zisk/v1.3.1-alpha/ziskup/ziskup -o ~/.zisk/bin/ziskup
chmod +x ~/.zisk/bin/ziskup
mkdir -p temp/runtime && cd temp/runtime
~/.zisk/bin/ziskup --version 1.3.1-alpha --gpu --provingkey
cd - && source ~/.bashrc
cargo-zisk-dev check-setup --proving-key ~/.zisk/provingKey --gpu
```

`ziskup` installs ZisK into `~/.zisk` and the proving key into `~/.zisk/provingKey`. It downloads the key tarball into the current directory, which is why the script changes into `temp/runtime` first. Always pass `--version`. Without it, `ziskup` installs the latest release, and that release's key and binaries do not match the host.

`ziskup` runs `check-setup` with `-a`, which skips the recursive setups, so the last command checks them as well. You'll find the full package list and the fixes for Ubuntu 25.10 in `docs/zisk-docs.md` on the branch.

### Guest and host build

```bash
make z6m_guest_zisk
(cd prover/prover_zisk && cargo build --release --no-default-features --features gpu)
```

The guest lands in `prover/guest_zisk/build/z6m_guest.elf` and the GPU host in `prover/prover_zisk/target/release/z6m_prover_zisk`. Be careful with `make z6m_prover_zisk`, which writes a CPU-only host to the same path and replaces the GPU one.

### Block execution

Next, get the 200-block mainnet corpus and convert it to MFBD:

```bash
curl -L -o temp/200_benchmark_blocks.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm-testdata/releases/download/benchmark-200-spread/200_benchmark_blocks.tar.gz
tar xzf temp/200_benchmark_blocks.tar.gz -C temp && rm temp/200_benchmark_blocks.tar.gz
make sp1-benchmark-corpus
```

The bundles land in `temp/200_benchmark_blocks_mfbd_v2/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd`. Now you can execute one block under `ziskemu`:

```bash
P=prover/prover_zisk/target/release/z6m_prover_zisk
$P --executor ziskemu execute \
  --file-name temp/200_benchmark_blocks_mfbd_v2/24545295/flatWitnessBundle24545295.mfbd
```

`execute` needs no proving key. It prints an `Executed block` line and a `Public Values:` line to stdout, and with `--file-name` it prints the block number as 0. To run all 200 blocks and compare their public values with native `state_transition`, use `make zisk-emu-check`.

### Block proof

Before you prove anything, keep temporary files on disk. The ZisK SDK writes them to `/tmp`, which is often in RAM.

```bash
export TMPDIR=$PWD/temp/runtime/tmp && mkdir -p "$TMPDIR" temp/proofs
P=prover/prover_zisk/target/release/z6m_prover_zisk
$P setup
$P prove --file-name temp/200_benchmark_blocks_mfbd_v2/24545295/flatWitnessBundle24545295.mfbd \
  --proof-path temp/proofs/24545295.bin
$P verify --proof-path temp/proofs/24545295.bin
```

The proof lands in `temp/proofs/24545295.bin`, and `prove` also appends a line to `temp/provingLogs.log`. Run `setup` once per guest ELF, because `verify` needs the program key it caches.

Each `prove` process loads the proving key again. When you want to prove many blocks, run them in one process:

```bash
mkdir -p temp/zisk_gpu_run && ln -sfn ../200_benchmark_blocks_mfbd_v2 temp/zisk_gpu_run/blocks
$P --test-service --data-dir temp/zisk_gpu_run \
  --start-block 24491136 --end-block 24640322 --prove-every 1
```

Proofs land in `temp/zisk_gpu_run/<N>/proof<N>.bin`, with one log line each in `temp/zisk_gpu_run/provingLogs.log`.

## Inputs and outputs

The host reads MFBD bundles by path, or from `<data-dir>/blocks/<N>/` in `--test-service` mode. The guest commits 112 bytes of public values in the same layout as the Hypercube guest, placed in ZisK output slots 0 to 27. [Proof guarantees](../inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees.md) gives the layout.

`prove` writes the proof to `--proof-path`. The default proof type is `compressed`, which ZisK calls VadcopFinal.

## Host checks

`prove` verifies each new proof before it saves it, and `verify` checks a proof against the program key from the setup cache. For the public values, `tools/scripts/zisk_execute.py` and `make zisk-emu-check` compare them with native `state_transition`.

Inside the guest, every free-input hint from a ZisK precompile is checked. A bad inverse, square root or division hint halts the guest, so no proof can exist. A bad GLV hint simply falls back to plain code.

## Known limits

- PR #86 is a draft based on alpha.6, so it lacks the changes merged to `main` after alpha.6.
- No release ships ZisK files.
- CI is execute-only. Both ZisK workflows run the guest under `ziskemu`, with no proving key, no GPU and no proofs.
- There has been one GPU run so far, on one RTX 5090 with `compressed` proofs.
- The `minimal` and `plonk` proof types, more than one GPU, the `assembly` executor, `--remote`, and `--service` against a live node are all untested.
- On EEST at tests@v21.0.1, 12,253 of 12,266 fixtures pass, 10 are skipped for exceeding the 20 MB size cap, and three fail.
- Two of those failures need more than ZisK's fixed 512 MiB of RAM. The third, `tx_invalid_first_in_block`, also failed on SP1 at alpha.6. PR #141 on `main` fixes it, but the branch doesn't have that fix.
- Ethproofs posting for ZisK is deferred.
- `--executor ziskemu` is execute-only, and `prove` with it exits 1.
- `ziskemu` exits 0 even when the guest halts with an error, so check stderr for `finished with error`.
- The prover fills the VRAM of a 32 GB card, and the host doesn't yet expose `max_streams` or `minimal_memory` for smaller cards.

## Measured

PR #86 reports one GPU run, on 2026-10-08, in which one RTX 5090 proved 200 of 200 corpus blocks at a median proving time of 31.5 s. Since ZisK has no release, [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md) lists no ZisK figures.

## Further reading

- [Choosing a prover](./choosing-a-prover.md)
- [Hypercube prover](./hypercube-prover.md)
- [Execution spec tests](../testing/execution-spec-tests.md)
- [PR #86](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/pull/86)
- [`docs/zisk-docs.md` on `som/zisk-impl`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/som/zisk-impl/docs/zisk-docs.md)

# Ethproofs posting

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/provers/ethproofs-posting

_The Airbender and Hypercube services report each proved block to Ethproofs once an endpoint, a token and a cluster id are set._

# Ethproofs posting

This page shows you how to make the Airbender or Hypercube service report its proofs to Ethproofs, and what it sends along the way.

[Ethproofs](https://ethproofs.org) collects proofs of Ethereum blocks from registered proving clusters. The Airbender and Hypercube services can both report to it, but the ZisK backend can't yet.

## Live clusters

One Zilkworm cluster posts today, "Zilkworm Airbender v3 2x5090 on-prem". It was the only one on [ethproofs.org/provers](https://ethproofs.org/provers) when checked on 2026-10-26. The Hypercube service has the same posting code, but no Zilkworm Hypercube cluster posts.

## Three settings

You turn posting on with three settings, and you need all three:

- `--ethproofs-endpoint`: the API base URL. The service appends paths such as `/proofs/queued` to it.
- `--ethproofs-token`: the API token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
- `--ethproofs-cluster-id`: the numeric cluster id.

If any of them is unset, the service still proves but posts nothing. Posting only happens in `--service` mode, because the `prove` subcommands of both binaries never post. Both binaries also accept `--post-every`, though neither uses it.

The examples in `docs/airbender-docker-service.md` and `prover/prover_airbender/README.md` use the staging API, `https://staging--ethproofs.netlify.app/api/v0`. In the commands below, replace `<endpoint>` with the URL Ethproofs gives your cluster.

Each binary takes the settings in its own way:

- `z6m_prover_hypercube` reads the three flags only.
- `z6m_prover_airbender` reads the flags or the variables `ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT`, `ETHPROOFS_TOKEN` and `ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID`.
- The Airbender image reads the three variables. If one is missing, its entrypoint unsets all three and logs that nothing is posted.

## Posting lifecycle

For each block it proves, the service sends three POST requests:

1. `/proofs/queued` when the service picks the block, before it waits for the prover.
2. `/proofs/proving` when proving starts.
3. `/proofs/proved` after a successful proof.

`queued` and `proving` carry only `block_number` and `cluster_id`. `proved` carries five fields:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `block_number` | The block number |
| `cluster_id` | The cluster id |
| `proving_time` | Proving time in milliseconds, measured by the host |
| `proving_cycles` | The guest's cycle count |
| `proof` | The proof file, base64-encoded |

The proof file is `proof.bin` for Airbender and `proof<N>.bin` for Hypercube. For Airbender, `proving_time` leaves out fetching, witness conversion and the preflight. Airbender also posts a proof only after the preflight and the proof both commit the expected block hash.

Each request has a 60 s timeout, and `queued` and `proving` go out once. A `proved` post that gets a 429, a 5xx or no answer is tried up to four times in all. After a 429, the service waits as long as the body's `retryAfter` or the `Retry-After` header asks, or 30 s by default. After a 5xx or no answer it waits 10 s, and no wait is longer than 120 s. If a retry gets a 409, an earlier attempt already landed, so the service stops there.

Other errors are logged and not retried. Posts run in the background and never hold up proving, and a failed post leaves the proof on disk.

## Cluster and verification key

Ethproofs checks a cluster's proofs against the key registered for it. If your cluster runs the Airbender image, register `z6m_guest_airbender.vk` from the same release:

```bash
curl -LO https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/releases/download/v0.1.0-alpha.7/z6m_guest_airbender.vk
sha256sum z6m_guest_airbender.vk
```

The alpha.7 release notes give its sha256 as `ffcdff786029d7f9621ad8c23ece641de9d72c38ecb1097d1d4b5e3e583c1de5`. When your cluster moves to a new release image, it needs that release's key. On first start, the image's entrypoint also computes a key and logs its sha256.

## Command examples

### Airbender image

```bash
export RPC_URL=http://<execution-client>:8545
export ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT=<endpoint>
export ETHPROOFS_TOKEN=<api-token>
export ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID=<cluster-id>
docker run -d --name zilkworm-airbender --gpus all --restart unless-stopped \
  -v /srv/zilkworm-airbender:/data \
  -e RPC_URL -e PROVE_EVERY=100 \
  -e ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT -e ETHPROOFS_TOKEN -e ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID \
  ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-airbender:v0.1.0-alpha.7
```

When posting is on, the entrypoint logs `posting to Ethproofs at` with the endpoint and cluster id. Proofs land in `/srv/zilkworm-airbender/proofs/<N>/proof.bin`, and [Airbender prover](./airbender-prover.md) covers the rest of the service.

### Hypercube binary

```bash
export RPC_URL=http://<execution-client>:8545
export ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT=<endpoint>
export ETHPROOFS_TOKEN=<api-token>
export ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID=<cluster-id>
SP1_PROVER=cuda ./z6m_prover_hypercube --service \
  --rpc-url "$RPC_URL" --data-dir data --prove-every 100 \
  --ethproofs-endpoint "$ETHPROOFS_ENDPOINT" \
  --ethproofs-token "$ETHPROOFS_TOKEN" \
  --ethproofs-cluster-id "$ETHPROOFS_CLUSTER_ID"
```

Proofs land in `data/<N>/proof<N>.bin`, and [Hypercube prover](./hypercube-prover.md) covers the rest of the service.

## Further reading

- [Airbender prover](./airbender-prover.md)
- [Hypercube prover](./hypercube-prover.md)
- [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md)
- [`prover/common/src/ethproofs_client.rs`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/prover/common/src/ethproofs_client.rs)
- [`docs/airbender-docker-service.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/airbender-docker-service.md)

# Execution pipeline

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/inside-the-guest/execution-pipeline

_A host feeds a block and its witness to a RISC-V guest, the guest commits public values, and the proof ties them to one guest ELF._

# Execution pipeline

This page follows a block from the node to the proof, so you know which program does what and where the state comes from.

Zilkworm is a C++ program that runs Ethereum blocks without a state database. It is compiled to RISC-V once per zkVM, and the zkVM runs that guest program and proves the run.

## Four steps from block to proof

1. The host fetches a block and its execution witness from a node and packs them into one input buffer for the guest. On the ERE path, the harness passes a fixture's `statelessInputBytes` through unchanged instead.
2. The zkVM runs the guest on that input. The guest anchors the pre-state to the parent header's state root and runs every transaction. Then it checks the header's state root and gas used against the run.
3. The guest commits a short, fixed record of the result as its public values. Depending on the guest, that record holds state roots, the block hash, gas used or a validation flag.
4. The zkVM proves the run. The proof ties the public values to one guest ELF through that ELF's verifying key.

[Witness formats](./witness-formats.md) describes the inputs, and [Proof guarantees](./proof-guarantees.md) lists each guest's public values and what a proof leaves out.

## Host and guest

Each zkVM integration has two programs, a host and a guest. The host is Rust, under `prover/prover_*`, and it runs natively. It fetches blocks over JSON-RPC, builds the input and drives the zkVM. In service mode it can also post proofs to Ethproofs.

The guest is a bare-metal RISC-V program under `prover/guest_*`, with no operating system running underneath it. All it does is read the input, call the C++ core and commit the public values.

That core, `zilk_core`, is one C++23 library. It started as a fork of Silkworm's core, covering execution, state, protocol rules, trie, RLP and types. You can build it natively for development and tests, and for each zkVM it is cross-compiled into that zkVM's guest with the xPack `riscv-none-elf-gcc` toolchain.

The two shipped hosts find their guest in different ways. The Hypercube host embeds its guest ELF at compile time, since `prover/prover_hypercube/build.rs` points `include_elf!` at the ELF that `make z6m_guest` builds. The Airbender host loads its guest image from the path in `--guest-bin`. Both hosts also link C++ code directly: their fetcher converts a node's witness to MFBD through the `prover/witness_ffi` bridge.

## Transaction execution with evmone

Zilkworm embeds evmone to execute transactions, and its fork, ZVM1, lives in `third_party/evmone`. The split is simple. The Zilkworm core handles blocks, the witness, state and the trie, and it calls evmone once per transaction. So evmone is one component of the guest, not the guest itself.

Most of the zkVM-specific acceleration for hashing and curve math sits in evmone's precompile code. [Precompiles and syscalls](./precompiles-and-syscalls.md) lists it per zkVM.

## Guest targets

Each zkVM gets its own guest build, and the zkVM sets the ISA.

| Guest | Source and build | ISA (`-march`) | Inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hypercube MFBD guest, SP1 | `prover/guest_hypercube`, `make z6m_guest` | `rv64im` | MFBD, EJSN |
| HashState guest, SP1 | `prover/guest_hypercube`, `make z6m_guest_slib` | `rv64im` | `statelessInputBytes`, EJSN |
| Airbender guest | `prover/guest_airbender`, `make z6m_guest_airbender` | `rv32im_zicsr` | MFBD, EJSN |
| ZisK guest, draft PR #86 | `prover/guest_zisk`, `make z6m_guest_zisk` | `rv64im_zicsr_zba_zbb_zbs_zbkb` | MFBD, EJSN |

Airbender's proving machine has only the unsigned multiply and divide instructions, so its guest avoids `mulh`, `mulhsu`, `div` and `rem`. A post-link check, `prover/guest_airbender/cmake/check_unsigned_muldiv.cmake`, guards this in the build.

The ZisK guest exists only on [PR #86](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/pull/86), a draft based on alpha.6, and no release ships it.

## DirectState and HashState

Zilkworm has two state backends, and the backend decides which input a guest takes.

DirectState is the default. It reads an MFBD bundle in place: accounts, storage, code and trie nodes sit in flat sections the guest does not decode. The run takes the pre-state root from the parent header that the first block names. When the block ends, the trie fold binds each touched key's pre-value to that root and recomputes the post-state root, which must match the header. The Hypercube MFBD guest, the Airbender and ZisK guests and the native runner all use DirectState.

HashState takes the EIP-8025 `statelessInputBytes` unchanged and checks as it goes. It walks each trie path from the parent state root at the moment of the read, so every read is checked against that root. If the witness can't confirm a read, either as a value or as a proven absence, the block is rejected. After the run, the guest folds the block's writes over the parent root and accepts only on a matching root.

The backend is fixed at compile time with `-DZ6M_HASH_STATE=ON`, and there is no runtime switch. That HashState build is the ERE guest, released as `stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1-<SP1 version>.elf`.

## Further reading

- [Witness formats](./witness-formats.md)
- [Proof guarantees](./proof-guarantees.md)
- [Precompiles and syscalls](./precompiles-and-syscalls.md)
- [Choosing a prover](../provers/choosing-a-prover.md)
- [`docs/hashstate.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/hashstate.md): the HashState backend in depth

# Witness formats

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/inside-the-guest/witness-formats

_Guests read MFBD bundles, raw SSZ statelessInputBytes or EJSN-wrapped test fixtures, and each format has its own producers._

# Witness formats

This page shows you the three input formats a guest reads, how a guest tells them apart, and which tools produce each one.

A stateless run needs the block and the part of the state it touches. The host hands the guest all of it in one byte buffer, and the guest reads the first bytes of that buffer to pick a path.

## MFBD bundles

An MFBD file is a 16-byte envelope followed by one or more flat bundles. The envelope is `<u32 magic><u32 version><u64 count>`, with magic `MFBD` (`0x4442464D`) and version 1. Each bundle then starts with a 56-byte header, magic `FBND` (`0x444E4246`), which points at six sections. Those hold the genesis block, the blocks to run, the ancestor headers, the pre-state, the trie nodes and the network name. The guest reads each section where it lies instead of decoding it.

The bundle version is `kFlatBundleVersion` in `zilk_core/core/types_zz/flat_bundle.hpp`, now 14. `load_flat_bundle` rejects any other version, so a stale bundle fails right away.

## Raw statelessInputBytes

The HashState guest takes the EIP-8025 `statelessInputBytes`, the SSZ `StatelessInput` that tests-zkevm fixtures carry, with no wrapper. Its first two bytes are the schema id `0x1501`, big-endian, so the buffer starts `0x15 0x01`. That keeps it easy to spot, because no other input magic starts with `0x15`.

## EJSN test fixtures

EJSN wraps one EEST `blockchain_test` JSON fixture for a guest. Its 8-byte header holds the magic `EJSN` (`0x4E534A45`) and version 1, and the minified JSON follows. The hosts wrap a fixture this way when you pass `--is-test`, and the native runner wraps `.json` files itself. Under HashState, the guest reads each block's `statelessInputBytes` field from that JSON.

## Producers and consumers

| Format | Wire marker | Produced by | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| MFBD | `MFBD` v1 envelope, `FBND` v14 bundles | The host fetcher, through `prover/witness_ffi`; the CLIs `json_witness_to_flat_bundle`, `eest_to_flat_bundle` and `legacy_to_flat_bundle` | DirectState guests, native `state_transition`, the QEMU runner |
| `statelessInputBytes` | First bytes `0x15 0x01` | tests-zkevm fixtures from ethereum/execution-specs; ERE's `witness-generator-cli` | The HashState guest under ere-hosts; the native HashState tests, inside fixture JSON |
| EJSN | `EJSN` v1, 8-byte header | `z6m_prover --is-test`, `z6m_prover_airbender --is-test`, the native runner | Every guest, and native `state_transition` |
| Legacy unified RLP | None | The old fetcher | `legacy_to_flat_bundle` only |

The three CLIs live in `zilk_core/dev/cli`. `json_witness_to_flat_bundle` converts a node's `debug_executionWitness` JSON, and the host links the same converter. `eest_to_flat_bundle` converts EEST fixtures with `emit` or `bulk-convert`, and `legacy_to_flat_bundle` converts old `unifiedBlockAndStateRlp<N>.bin` files.

## Formats each guest accepts

| Guest | Accepts | Any other input |
|---|---|---|
| Hypercube MFBD guest | MFBD, EJSN | Raw SSZ fails with "needs the HashState guest". Unknown magic fails the run. |
| HashState guest | Raw SSZ, EJSN | MFBD fails, since its path is compiled out. Anything else gives the all-zero result. |
| Airbender guest | MFBD, EJSN | Same as the Hypercube MFBD guest |
| ZisK guest, draft PR #86 | MFBD, EJSN | Same as the Hypercube MFBD guest |
| Native `state_transition` | `.mfbd` files, `.json` files wrapped as EJSN | Release builds lack HashState, so raw SSZ fails |

## Legacy unified RLP

`unifiedBlockAndStateRlp<N>.bin` files carry no magic, and no current guest reads them. They still matter in two places. `legacy_to_flat_bundle` converts them to MFBD, and `make sp1-benchmark-corpus` runs that conversion. The Airbender host also falls back to that file name when a block has no `.mfbd` file, so convert old data first.

## Spec documents

The MFBD spec, `docs/mfbd_design_specs.md`, is normative: it says what a producer and a verifier must check. `docs/flat_witness_bundle.md` is the byte-layout reference. One diagram in the spec still says `FBND` v13, but its section 4.2 and the code say 14.

## Further reading

- [Execution pipeline](./execution-pipeline.md)
- [Proof guarantees](./proof-guarantees.md)
- [`docs/mfbd_design_specs.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/mfbd_design_specs.md): the normative MFBD spec
- [`docs/flat_witness_bundle.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/flat_witness_bundle.md): the envelope and bundle byte layout
- [`docs/hashstate.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/hashstate.md): how HashState parses `statelessInputBytes`

# Precompiles and syscalls

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/inside-the-guest/precompiles-and-syscalls

_Each guest hands hashing and big-number math to its zkVM's circuits, through SP1 ecalls or Airbender and ZisK CSRs._

# Precompiles and syscalls

This page shows you where each guest hands work to its zkVM's dedicated circuits, which call reaches which circuit, and what stays in plain RISC-V code.

Hashing and curve math take many RISC-V instructions, and a zkVM proves every instruction it runs, so plain code for these routines makes a long trace. That is why each zkVM offers dedicated circuits for them. The guest reaches a circuit through an `ecall` on SP1, or through a CSR access on Airbender and ZisK. Each such call replaces a software routine the prover would otherwise trace cycle by cycle.

## SP1 ecalls

Both Hypercube guests declare their ecalls in `prover/guest_hypercube/src/include/sp1_syscalls.hpp`. Most wrappers are always inlined and compile to a single `ecall`, and most call sites sit in ZVM1, the evmone fork in `third_party/evmone`.

| Ecalls | Called from | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `keccak_permute` | `lib/evmone_precompiles/keccak.c` | Every Keccak-256 hash: KECCAK256, trie nodes, addresses |
| `sha256_extend`, `sha256_compress` | `lib/evmone_precompiles/sha256.cpp` | The SHA256 precompile, and the public-values digest |
| `secp256k1_add`, `secp256k1_double` | `lib/evmone_precompiles/secp256k1.cpp` | ECRECOVER and transaction sender recovery |
| `uint256_mulmod` | `lib/evmone/instructions.hpp`, `lib/evmone_precompiles/modexp.cpp` | ADDMOD, MULMOD and MODEXP |
| `bn254_fp_*mod`, `bn254_fp2_*mod` | `lib/evmone_precompiles/modarith.hpp`, `pairing/field_template.hpp` | Field math for ECADD, ECMUL and ECPAIRING |
| `bn254_add`, `bn254_double` | evmone's precompile dispatch, `test/state/precompiles.cpp` | Point math for ECADD and ECMUL |
| `bls12381_fp_*mod`, `bls12381_fp2_*mod` | `cmake/patch_blst_sp1.sh`, a build-time patch of blst | The BLS12-381 precompiles and KZG point evaluation |

The header also declares ecalls that nothing in the guest calls at the current ZVM1 pin. Those are the secp256r1 and ed25519 point ecalls, `bls12381_add` and `bls12381_double`, `u256x2048_mul`, and the two `uint256_*_with_carry` calls.

Public values take a different route. The guest commits them by writing to file descriptor 13, `SP1_FD_PUBLIC_VALUES`, and the runtime in `prover/guest_hypercube/src/sp1_runtime.cpp` buffers those bytes. At halt it hashes them with SHA-256 and commits the digest.

## Airbender CSRs

The Airbender guest reaches its delegation circuits by writing to CSRs, which `prover/guest_airbender/src/include/airbender_csr.hpp` names.

| CSR | Name | Use in the guest |
|---|---|---|
| `0x7C0` | Non-determinism oracle | Reads the input words and writes log output |
| `0x7CA` | BigInt | 256-bit add, subtract, multiply, compare and copy |
| `0x7CC`, `0x7CD`, `0x7CE` | keccak_f1600: theta and rho, column parity, chi5 | One Keccak permutation per run of writes |
| `0x7C7` | Blake2s | Declared only; no guest code calls it |

The curve and scalar logic around these calls stays RISC-V code in ZVM1. The alpha.5 release notes map each precompile to a delegation:

| Precompile | Delegation | Code path |
|---|---|---|
| ECRECOVER, and every transaction's sender recovery | BigInt | evmone's secp256k1, with Montgomery field arithmetic on BigInt |
| SHA256, RIPEMD160, IDENTITY, BLAKE2F | None | Plain rv32 code |
| MODEXP | BigInt | Montgomery exponentiation for 256-bit operands; the generic path otherwise |
| ECADD, ECMUL, ECPAIRING | BigInt | bn254 field arithmetic |
| POINT_EVALUATION and the BLS12-381 precompiles | BigInt | blst, patched at build time to multiply on BigInt |
| P256VERIFY | BigInt | evmone's generic Montgomery field template |
| KECCAK256, and every hash the guest computes | keccak_f1600 | One delegation run per permutation |

BigInt also carries the EVM's own 256-bit add, subtract and multiply, along with its 32-byte copies.

## ZisK CSRs on PR #86

The ZisK guest exists only on [draft PR #86](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/pull/86). It calls ZisK's CSR precompiles, in the range `0x800` to `0x819`, and its `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset` and `memcmp` go to ZisK's DMA precompiles.

| Area | ZisK precompiles |
|---|---|
| keccak-f | `0x800` |
| SHA256 | `0x805` |
| ADDMOD, MULMOD, and MODEXP up to 32-byte operands | `0x802` |
| ECRECOVER | `0x802`, `0x803`, `0x804`, plus square-root, inverse and GLV-split hints |
| ECADD, ECMUL, ECPAIRING | `0x802`, `0x806`, `0x807`, `0x808` to `0x80A` |
| BLS12-381 and KZG, through patched blst | `0x80B`, `0x80E` to `0x810`, plus an inverse hint |
| BLAKE2F | `0x819` |
| P256VERIFY | `0x802`, `0x817`, `0x818`, plus an inverse hint |
| Memory copy, set and compare | DMA `0x813`, `0x814`, `0x816` |
| EVM ADD, MUL, EXP, MOD | `0x811` for ADD, `0x801` for MUL and EXP, `0x802` for MOD |

RIPEMD160, IDENTITY and MODEXP with operands over 32 bytes stay in software. DIV, SDIV and SMOD use a division hint that the guest checks.

Hints deserve a closer look. A hint, or fcall, returns a value the prover supplies freely, so the guest checks every hint before it uses the result. A bad inverse, square-root or division hint halts the run with an error, and no proof can exist. The one exception is a bad GLV-split hint: the guest just falls back to the software split, which needs no hint.

## Further reading

- [Execution pipeline](./execution-pipeline.md)
- [ZisK prover](../provers/zisk-prover.md)
- [`prover/guest_hypercube/src/include/sp1_syscalls.hpp`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/prover/guest_hypercube/src/include/sp1_syscalls.hpp): the SP1 ecall declarations
- [`docs/airbender_architecture.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/airbender_architecture.md): the Airbender guest, its memory map and CSR delegations

# Proof guarantees

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees

_Each guest commits a fixed public-values layout, each host checks it to a different degree, and the verifying key ties a proof to one guest ELF._

# Proof guarantees

This page tells you what a Zilkworm proof lets you trust, guest by guest, and what you still have to check yourself.

A proof says that one guest ELF ran on some input and committed some public values. The verifying key names the ELF, and the public values say what the run found. What you can trust depends on both, and on how much the host checks.

## Public values per guest

### Hypercube MFBD guest, 112 bytes

A release publishes this guest as `z6m_guest_hypercube_mfbd`, and it commits 112 bytes.

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8 | `gas_used` | Gas used, little-endian. A failed run writes `UINT64_MAX` and a skipped run `UINT64_MAX - 1`. |
| 8 | 32 | `pre_state_root` | The parent state root the run starts from |
| 40 | 32 | `post_state_root` | The state root after the last block |
| 72 | 32 | `block_hash` | The hash of the last block |
| 104 | 8 | `chain_id` | The chain ID, little-endian |

The ZisK guest on draft PR #86 commits the same 112 bytes, in ZisK output slots 0 to 27.

### HashState guest, 43 bytes

The HashState guest is the ERE guest, `stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1-<SP1 version>`. On `statelessInputBytes` input, it commits the SSZ `StatelessValidationResult`.

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 32 | `new_payload_request_root` | The root of the block's `NewPayloadRequest` |
| 32 | 1 | `successful_validation` | 1 if the guest accepted the block, else 0 |
| 33 | 8 | `chain_id` | The chain ID, little-endian |
| 41 | 2 | `schema_id` | The input schema id, little-endian |

A rejected block still yields a result, with `successful_validation` set to 0. Only an input that does not decode gives the all-zero result. On EJSN input, the same guest writes the 112-byte layout above instead.

### Airbender guest, 32 bytes

The Airbender guest commits the hash of the last block it validated. It writes the hash's bytes in order, as little-endian words, to registers `a0` to `a7`. Small as it is, that hash binds the parent's state root and the block's post-state root, gas used and receipts root.

The value is zero when the run validated no block, which happens on an EJSN success or on an MFBD whose every block is flagged expected-invalid. A failed or skipped run ends at `finish_error` and commits nothing, so it cannot be proven.

## Checks inside the guest

Before a DirectState guest commits, it checks the chain it ran. It takes the pre-state root from the parent header that the first block names and requires each later block to extend the one before it. It also checks each header's state root and gas used against the run.

An MFBD envelope can hold several bundles, each its own chain. In that case the public values cover only the last validated block's bundle.

The HashState guest checks that the witness headers chain by parent hash and end at the block's parent. Every account and storage read is checked against the parent state root. The guest rejects the block on a read it cannot confirm, or on a malformed witness, and it accepts the block only if the folded post-state root matches the header.

## Checks in each host

The hosts check the public values to very different degrees:

- The Airbender host derives the expected block hash from the input. When the guest commits another, it fails `execute`, `prove`, `verify`, `--test-service` and `--service`.
- The Hypercube host parses the 112 bytes and logs them, but it does not compare them with the input or with a node.
- The ERE harness, ere-hosts, compares the 43 bytes with the fixture's `statelessOutputBytes` and records the result as `output_matched`.

So if you need a Hypercube proof to match the chain, compare `block_hash` and `post_state_root` with a node yourself.

## Keys and guest builds

The verifying key is derived from the guest ELF, so every new guest build gets a new key. Each release publishes the key of each guest right next to the guest.

Build flags count too. The Hypercube MFBD guest is built with `USE_HASH_KEY=OFF` and the Airbender guest with `USE_HASH_KEY=ON`, and the key depends on that flag. The Airbender key also depends on the recursion verifier programs, and its prover accepts only their default `RECURSION_*_BLAKE` modes.

Keys can also rotate without any guest change, when the zkVM itself moves. SP1 v6.9.0 loads a guest's initial memory differently from v6.6.0, so SP1 keys published for alpha.6 do not verify alpha.7 proofs. In the same release, a DirectState runner fix changed the MFBD and Airbender keys but left the ERE guest's key alone.

:::warning
Verify a proof with the key from the release that built its guest. Keys can change between releases even when the guest code does not.
:::

## Out of scope

A proof covers execution of the input it was given, and nothing more. It does not cover:

- Consensus validity. Nothing in the proof says the block is canonical or attested.
- Blob availability. The guest never sees blob data, so the proof cannot say the blobs were published.
- The parent header's origin. The guest anchors to the parent header in its input, so a verifier checks the committed roots or block hash against a trusted node.

## Further reading

- [Execution pipeline](./execution-pipeline.md)
- [Witness formats](./witness-formats.md)
- [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md)
- [Ethproofs posting](../provers/ethproofs-posting.md)
- [`docs/architecture.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/architecture.md): the input envelope and the 112- and 32-byte layouts

# Execution spec tests

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/testing/execution-spec-tests

_Zilkworm runs the Ethereum execution spec tests natively and inside the Hypercube and Airbender guests, on a checksum-pinned fixture release._

# Execution spec tests

By the end of this page you can run the Ethereum execution spec tests against Zilkworm yourself. You will also know how CI runs them inside the zkVMs.

The Ethereum Execution Spec Tests, or EESTs, are the test vectors for the Ethereum execution layer. They are generated from the execution specs and cover every fork plus many edge cases, so a failing test usually points to a consensus bug. The fixtures ship as releases of [ethereum/execution-specs](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/releases), and the docs live at [eest.ethereum.org](https://eest.ethereum.org/). CI runs them natively and inside two zkVMs.

## Fixture pins

The fixtures come from release tarballs, pinned by checksum. A manifest, `test-fixtures.json`, names each tarball's URL, sha256 and size, along with the paths to extract. It has one entry, `eest_stable`, which pins `tests@v21.0.1` with sha256 `b9b14391ed1a625e4ca9a058c055d0eacd98a42b76c7a6127c640cdc2d3c9439` and extracts `fixtures/blockchain_tests`. You fetch them with one command:

```bash
make test-fixtures
```

This runs `tools/test-fixtures.sh`, which downloads each tarball, checks its sha256 and extracts it into `test-fixtures-cache/<key>/`. A rerun does nothing while the pin matches. To move a pin, edit `test-fixtures.json`.

The HashState suite is the exception. It uses a second release, `tests-zkevm@v21.0.6`, which the Makefile downloads with `gh release download`, so that one is not checksum-pinned.

## Native run

To run `make eest-blockchain-tests` you need CMake, Ninja, ctest, a C++23 compiler, Git, Python 3, curl and tar. You do not need Rust for it. Only the targets that build `z6m_prover`, such as `selftest` and `eest-prover-test`, need Rust. [Building from source](../reference/building-from-source.md) lists the toolchain.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm
cd zilkworm
git submodule update --init --recursive
make eest-blockchain-tests
```

The target first fetches the pinned tarball and converts every JSON fixture to MFBD with `eest_to_flat_bundle bulk-convert`. The converted set lands in `test-fixtures-cache/mfbd-<sha>/`, named after the pin. A rerun skips the fetch and the conversion as long as the pin and the converter binary stay the same. Then the target builds with `-DBUILD_TESTING=ON` and runs `ctest --parallel`, one case per fixture file.

## Make targets

| Target | What it does |
|---|---|
| `make test-fixtures` | Downloads, checks and extracts the pinned tarballs |
| `make selftest` | Converts one fixture, `add11`, to MFBD and runs it with `z6m_prover execute` |
| `make eest-blockchain-tests` | Runs the converted MFBD set through native ctest |
| `make eest-blockchain-tests-json` | Runs native ctest on the JSON fixtures, with no conversion |
| `make eest-prover-test` | Runs the MFBD set through `z6m_prover --test-service`, under the SP1 executor |
| `make eest-prover-test-json` | Runs the JSON fixtures through `z6m_prover --test-service` |
| `make eest-zkevm-tests` | Runs the `tests-zkevm@v21.0.6` fixtures through a native HashState build in `build/zkevm` |

Skip `make tests` and `make tests-json`. Both are broken, because they pass `--execution-log-dir`, a flag `z6m_prover` does not have.

## Runs inside the zkVMs

CI also runs the pinned set inside the guests, in two workflows. The HyperCube EEST Blockchain Tests workflow builds `z6m_prover` and runs the MFBD set through `tools/scripts/eest_runner.py` under the SP1 executor; that job fails above a set failure threshold. The Airbender EEST Blockchain Tests workflow builds the Airbender guest and host, then runs `make eest` in `prover/prover_airbender`. It fails only on failures outside the known-failures lists.

The native suite has its own workflow, EEST Blockchain Tests. The QEMU runs have a page of their own, [RISC-V tests under QEMU](./riscv-tests-under-qemu.md).

## Known failures

Two files track the fixtures that are expected to fail. The first, `zilk_core/dev/eest-known-failures.txt`, lists fixtures that the runner gets wrong on every target. Their ctests are registered `WILL_FAIL`, so a listed fixture that passes again shows up as a failure until you take it off the list. As of v0.1.0-alpha.7 that list holds only its header, which means the native suite expects no failures.

The second, `prover/prover_airbender/eest-known-failures.txt`, lists 25 fixtures that the Airbender guest does not finish. These are not wrong results. They hit resource limits such as the execution cycle cap. The Airbender job adds the native list to its own.

## State-root check before a release

Before a release, you re-run a directory of mainnet blocks natively with `tools/scripts/release_state_root_check.sh`. The script builds `state_transition` in Release mode and then runs every `<dir>/<N>/flatWitnessBundle<N>.mfbd` file in parallel. It reports each block whose output shows `ERROR: State Root Mismatch`, along with each timeout and each non-zero exit.

```bash
tools/scripts/release_state_root_check.sh --dir <blocks-dir> -j "$(nproc)"
```

Use `-s` and `-e` to limit the block range. Logs go to `temp/release_state_root_check/` unless you name another directory with `-l`.

## Further reading

- [RISC-V tests under QEMU](./riscv-tests-under-qemu.md)
- [ERE validation](./ere-validation.md)
- [Building from source](../reference/building-from-source.md)
- [Benchmarks and CI](../reference/benchmarks-and-ci.md)
- [`test-fixtures.json`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/test-fixtures.json): the fixture pin

# RISC-V tests under QEMU

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/testing/riscv-tests-under-qemu

_The execution spec tests also run on bare-metal rv32im and rv64im builds of the core under QEMU, to catch bugs that only show on RISC-V._

# RISC-V tests under QEMU

Here you will learn to run the spec tests on bare-metal RISC-V builds of the core, and what those runs catch that native runs miss.

A test should run as close to the real target as it can, and for Zilkworm the real target is a bare-metal RISC-V guest inside a zkVM. The QEMU runner in `qemu_runner/` builds the core for rv32im or rv64im. It then runs every [execution spec test](./execution-spec-tests.md) fixture on that build under QEMU.

## Requirements

The QEMU suite uses the same pinned fixtures as the native suite, from `test-fixtures.json`. You need:

- CMake, Ninja, ctest, Git, Python 3, curl and tar
- a C++23 host compiler, for the fixture converter
- QEMU's RISC-V system emulators, `qemu-system-misc` on Ubuntu
- Node.js and npm, to install the cross-compiler

Then install the cross-compiler, [xPack's RISC-V toolchain](https://xpack-dev-tools.github.io/riscv-none-elf-gcc-xpack/docs/install/). CI uses version 15.2.0-1.1:

```bash
npm i -g xpm
xpm install @xpack-dev-tools/riscv-none-elf-gcc@15.2.0-1.1 --global --verbose
export PATH=$HOME/.local/xPacks/@xpack-dev-tools/riscv-none-elf-gcc/15.2.0-1.1/.content/bin:$PATH
```

## Quickstart

Clone the repository and its submodule:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm
cd zilkworm
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

Then run the suite on rv32im:

```bash
cd qemu_runner
make eest-rv32
```

Like the native suite, the target fetches and converts the pinned fixtures. It then cross-compiles the core for rv32im, builds the test runner in `qemu_runner/build`, and has `ctest` start one `qemu-system-riscv32` instance per fixture.

For rv64im, run `make eest-rv64` instead; it builds in `qemu_runner/build64`. `make rerun-ctest` runs ctest again with verbose output and a longer per-test timeout, and you add `ARCH=rv64` to target rv64im. The QEMU ctests share the native known-failures list, `zilk_core/dev/eest-known-failures.txt`.

## CI workflows

In CI, two workflows run the suite: Qemu EESTs on RV32IM and Qemu EESTs on RV64IM. Each one runs on pushes and pull requests to `main`, `master` and `release/*`, on a cron every three days, and on demand. Both start from the `ghcr.io/erigontech/zilkworm-ci` image and add `qemu-system-misc`. Then they run `make xpack-elf-eest` and `make rerun-ctest`.

## Bugs that cross-architecture runs catch

The native suite catches logic and spec errors quickly. The QEMU runs catch the bugs that stay hidden on a 64-bit x86 host.

On rv32, `size_t`, `uintptr_t` and `long` are 32 bits wide, so truncation and overflow in size math show up. Alignment and struct-layout assumptions can break too. Because `rv32im` has no atomics and no floating point, an accidental use of either pulls in library code or breaks the link. Cost matters as well: a path that is cheap on x86_64 can turn out costly in instructions on rv32, and in a zkVM every instruction is proven.

One check is left to the Airbender build. The QEMU build is plain `rv32im`, so it does not check Airbender's ban on signed multiply and divide; the Airbender guest's post-link check covers that.

This gives you a quick way to read a failure. A test that fails both natively and under QEMU usually has a logic or spec error. One that fails only under QEMU points to a width, alignment or ISA issue.

## Further reading

- [Execution spec tests](./execution-spec-tests.md)
- [Execution pipeline](../inside-the-guest/execution-pipeline.md)
- [Benchmarks and CI](../reference/benchmarks-and-ci.md)
- [`qemu_runner/Makefile`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/qemu_runner/Makefile): the QEMU build and test targets

# ERE validation

Source: https://zilkworm.erigon.tech/testing/ere-validation

_The HashState guest runs in the ERE harness, which checks its output against each fixture and estimates its SP1 proving cost._

# ERE validation

This page explains how Zilkworm's HashState guest is checked in the ERE harness, and how you can run the same check and cost estimate yourself.

The zkEVM benchmark workload, [eth-act/zkevm-benchmark-workload](https://github.com/eth-act/zkevm-benchmark-workload), runs stateless-validator guests inside zkVMs through ERE, [eth-act/ere](https://github.com/eth-act/ere). Its `ere-hosts` tool runs a guest on each fixture. Zilkworm takes part as an execution client, with its HashState guest on SP1.

## The ERE guest

The ERE guest is the HashState build of the Hypercube guest, which `make z6m_guest_slib` builds with `-DZ6M_HASH_STATE=ON`. It takes each fixture's `statelessInputBytes` unchanged, with no host adapter in between. [Witness formats](../inside-the-guest/witness-formats.md) describes that input.

Releases publish the guest as `stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1-<version>.elf` and `.vk`, following the ere-guests handbook pattern `stateless-validator-<guest>-<zkVM>-<zkVM version>`. The version is the `sp1-sdk` tag that `derive_vk` builds against, read from `prover/stateless_validator/Cargo.toml`. For v0.1.0-alpha.7 that gives `stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1-v6.9.0.elf` and `.vk`.

## Checks per fixture

For each fixture, ere-hosts feeds the guest the fixture's `statelessInputBytes`, and the guest commits the 43-byte `StatelessValidationResult`. ere-hosts then compares those bytes with the fixture's `statelessOutputBytes` and records `output_matched`. [Proof guarantees](../inside-the-guest/proof-guarantees.md) gives the 43-byte layout.

A cost run works differently. It does not prove at all; it asks SP1 for an estimate of the proving cost instead. `tools/ere_compare.py` turns the per-fixture records into tables.

## Make targets

| Target | What it does |
|---|---|
| `make ere-bin` | Builds the HashState guest and derives its VK. Stages `build/ere-bin/stateless-validator-zilkworm-sp1.elf` and `.vk`. |
| `make ere-validate` | Runs every fixture in `ERE_INPUT_FOLDER` under ere-hosts, then checks `output_matched` with `ere_compare.py --validate` |
| `make ere-cost` | Runs ere-hosts with `--action estimate-cost`, then prints the cost table and report |
| `make ere-compare` | Runs `ere-cost`, then the same estimate for Reth's guest, and compares the two |
| `make ere-fixtures` | Generates EEST fixtures with `witness-generator-cli`; runs first only when `ERE_GEN_FIXTURES` is set |

The targets run `ere-hosts` inside a checkout of the benchmark workload, which you point to with `ERE_WORKLOAD_DIR`. Every run passes `--force-rerun`, so no stale result from an older guest survives. `ERE_IMAGE_REGISTRY` points ERE at its prebuilt zkVM images on `ghcr.io/eth-act/ere`.

To test a guest you built yourself, set `ERE_BIN_PATH` to its directory, such as `build/ere-bin`. `ere-bin-link` then links the files under the versioned name ere-hosts loads, and stops if the workload's SP1 version differs from the one `derive_vk` used. Leave `ERE_BIN_PATH` empty and ere-hosts downloads the published guest instead.

## Local run

To run this locally you need Rust and a container engine, because ere-hosts drives ERE's SP1 server in a container. For inputs, `tools/ere-fetch-fixtures.sh` fetches stateless fixtures from a public Sepolia block catalog and caches them under `test-fixtures-cache/ere-sepolia/`. Its `latest N` form extracts the N latest batches to `latest/`.

`ERE_WORKLOAD_DIR` must point at a workload checkout that has the `zilkworm` client. Today that means the `som/ere-v0.19.5` branch of the erigontech fork, which the first command below clones. Run every command from the Zilkworm repository root.

```bash
git clone --branch som/ere-v0.19.5 https://github.com/erigontech/zkevm-benchmark-workload ../zkevm-benchmark-workload_fork
make ere-bin
tools/ere-fetch-fixtures.sh latest 1
make ere-validate \
    ERE_WORKLOAD_DIR=../zkevm-benchmark-workload_fork \
    ERE_BIN_PATH=build/ere-bin \
    ERE_INPUT_FOLDER=$(pwd)/test-fixtures-cache/ere-sepolia/latest
```

To estimate cost instead, swap `ere-validate` for `ere-cost` or `ere-compare` and keep the same variables.

## ERE benchmark workflow

In CI, `.github/workflows/ere-benchmark.yml` runs the same targets. It runs on pushes to `release/*`, on demand, and when `release.yml` calls it after each `v*` release.

The guest can come from two sources. With `build`, the job runs `make ere-bin` at the run's ref; with `release`, it downloads the release's ERE guest and checks it against `SHA256SUMS.txt`. The job then fetches the latest batches of the public Sepolia catalog, one batch by default. It runs `ere-validate` and `ere-cost`, plus `ere-compare` when the `compare` input is on. The step summary holds the result tables, and the run uploads the per-fixture records as the `ere-metrics` artifact.

The workflow uses the erigontech forks of zkevm-benchmark-workload and ere-guests, on branch `som/ere-v0.19.5`. Those forks carry the Zilkworm client until it is upstreamed.

`release.yml` calls the workflow with `compare: false`, because ere-guests had no Reth SP1 v6.9.0 guest yet. By alpha.7 the fork registry had taken one, so `make ere-compare` runs on the forks again.

## Results

For the published ERE results and their release tags, see [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md). Each workflow run also keeps its own tables in its summary.

## Further reading

- [Releases and assets](../reference/releases-and-assets.md)

- [Execution spec tests](./execution-spec-tests.md)
- [`docs/ere_integration.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/ere_integration.md): harness setup, variables and past runs
- [`docs/hashstate.md`](https://github.com/erigontech/zilkworm/blob/main/docs/hashstate.md): the HashState backend
